361	
362	**What:** the 1.3.2 bump (above) added exactly one automated tripwire
363	(`GhosttyOrphanShellUITests.testNormalQuitLeavesNoOrphanedShell`) for `QA-libghostty.md` §N's
364	IO-layer subsection. Everything else in §N — surface/split churn volume, workroom switch, workroom
365	delete, force-quit variant, the scrollbar overlay — is still manual-only, exactly as it was before
366	this bump. That gap isn't new; it's just now visible with a name, having been walked end-to-end this
367	session rather than assumed.
368	
369	**Two concrete blockers surfaced while running the manual retest, worth fixing before the next
370	attempt at automating this, not just re-discovering them again:**
371	- **Workroom-tab chips and the run-command button (`workroom.tab.*`, `runCommand.run`) didn't respond
372	  to synthetic `AXPress` or a raw `click at {x,y}` from an external AppleScript-driven session** —
373	  0 observable effect despite the action reporting success and the on-screen bounds being correct.
374	  Real keyboard shortcuts (⌘R/⇧⌘R) and raw `keystroke` text input worked fine throughout, which is
375	  how the QA results file's Run-tab and behavioral checks actually got driven. `GhosttyOrphanShellUITests`
376	  and `GhosttyActionDispatchUITests` prove an actual XCUITest host process (not external AppleScript)
377	  CAN drive these controls — `focusTerminal`'s tab-chip click works there. So the fix for
378	  workroom-switch/delete/OSC-7 automation is likely "write it as a real XCUITest," not "find the
379	  right AppleScript incantation."
380	- **`Process()` spawning `/bin/ps` (or presumably anything) throws `NSPOSIXErrorDomain Code=1
381	  "Operation not permitted"` from inside an XCUITest runner** (`WorkroomAppUITests`'s auto-generated
382	  `XCTRunner` host is sandboxed against subprocess spawning; the app under test itself is not — two
383	  different sandbox realms). `GhosttyOrphanShellUITests` worked around this with a heartbeat FILE
384	  (`/tmp`, not `NSTemporaryDirectory()` — see that file's doc comment for why `NSTemporaryDirectory()`
385	  resolves to a different, container-private path in the runner vs. the app) instead of polling `ps`.
386	  Any future XCUITest needing to observe OS-level process state should reuse that pattern rather than
387	  rediscovering the `ps` restriction.
388	
389	**Also unverified, not automated, and not re-attempted manually either — flag before assuming
390	fine:** the terminfo `Se` capability's cursor-style-reset behavior change (`\E[2 q` → `\E[0 q`, found
391	during the bump's resource regen) has never been visually confirmed. A `screencapture -x` attempt at
392	this was abandoned mid-session when it turned out to capture the whole display rather than the
393	target window (see the bump entry above) — needs either a window-scoped capture API or a human at
394	the keyboard, not screen-wide automation.
395	
396	**Sharper target for whoever runs this, found while surveying the wider `332b2aef...35e1a016`
397	upstream range (not just the diff of the terminfo file itself):** the `Se` change isn't a one-time
398	fixed-escape swap. It was refined again after `\E[2 q`→`\E[0 q` — `Se` now restores whatever cursor
399	style/blink the engine is *configured* with, paired with new default-cursor-style/blink options
400	(ghostty `c19ce03b`, `42fcd58d`; both confirmed ancestors of our pinned `35e1a016`). So the right
401	check is "does resetting after a TUI exit return to Workroom's actual configured default," not
402	merely "does it emit `\E[0 q`" — a literal-escape assertion could pass while the dynamic-default
403	behavior is still unverified.
404	
405	**Depends on:** nothing blocking — can start anytime. The two platform-constraint findings above
406	mean whoever picks this up should design as a real XCUITest from the start, not attempt external
407	AppleScript driving again.
408	
409	**Priority:** P3 — the manual checklist still covers this; nothing is unguarded, just unautomated.
410	
411	### Wire native `selection_changed` notification (macapp) — CMT-3 follow-up, unblocked by the pin bump, filed 2026-08-14
412	
413	**What:** `GhosttySurfaceView.startAccessibilityPolling`/`pollAccessibilityContent`
414	(`GhosttySurfaceView.swift:990-1014`) drive VoiceOver's `.valueChanged`/`.selectedTextChanged` off a
415	400ms `Timer`, gated cheaply on `NSWorkspace.shared.isVoiceOverEnabled` checked first each tick. The
416	comment justifying the poll (lines 984-989) says libghostty has no per-frame content-changed callback
417	to hook instead — true when CMT-3 shipped (2026-08-10), on the pre-bump engine. **Confirmed stale
418	today** against the currently-linked header
419	(`DerivedData/Build/Products/Debug/include/libghostty/ghostty.h:953`):
420	`GHOSTTY_ACTION_SELECTION_CHANGED` exists on this exact pin, and `GhosttyRuntimeAdapter`'s action
421	switch (`GhosttyRuntimeAdapter.swift:25-126`, `default:` fallback at 127) has no case for it — grepped,
422	zero matches for `SELECTION_CHANGED` anywhere in `WorkroomApp` outside the vendored header.
423	
424	**Why:** replaces a 400ms poll with an engine-pushed event for the selection half of the a11y signal.
425	Selection changes get announced immediately instead of up to 400ms late, and the poll's
426	`readSelectionText()` call (the actual per-tick cost) only runs when the engine says something
427	changed, instead of unconditionally on every tick while VoiceOver is on. The `.valueChanged` side
428	(screen content) has no native hook in this action set and keeps polling — this only replaces the
429	selection half, exactly as the original CMT-3 entry anticipated ("after the pin bump it comes from the
430	engine as `GHOSTTY_ACTION_SELECTION_CHANGED`").
431	
432	**How to start:** the action carries no payload — checked the header's `ghostty_action_u` union, it has
433	no `selection_changed` field, so it's a bare tag. Add a `case GHOSTTY_ACTION_SELECTION_CHANGED:` to
434	`GhosttyRuntimeAdapter.handleAction` that resolves the view via `surfaceView(from: target)` and calls a
435	new `view.handleSelectionChanged()` doing what `pollAccessibilityContent` already does for the
436	selection half: `readSelectionText()`, diff against `lastAccessibilitySelectedText`, post
437	`.selectedTextChanged` on change. Leave the poll running for `.valueChanged` until/unless a
438	render-changed action shows up too.
439	
440	**Depends on:** nothing — the pin bump already landed (2026-08-13) and the header confirms the action
441	tag exists on this exact linked build.
442	
443	**Priority:** P3 — no user-visible regression today (the poll works correctly), but it's a small,
444	scoped cleanup the bump specifically unblocked, and the original CMT-3 entry already named it as the
445	reason to revisit.
446	
447	### `ghostty_surface_tty_name` is available and unused (macapp) — filed 2026-08-14
448	
449	**What:** the pin bump also exposes `ghostty_surface_tty_name` (confirmed in the currently-linked
450	header, `ghostty.h:1138`, right next to `ghostty_surface_foreground_pid` at `:1137` — which we DO
451	already consume, for agent-backend recognition at `GhosttySurfaceView.swift:41`). `tty_name` has zero
452	call sites anywhere in `WorkroomApp` (grepped).
453	
454	**Why it might matter:** session-daemon reattach and orphan-shell detection currently identify a pane's
455	process by foreground-pgid + argv0 heuristics. A tty name is a firmer, OS-level identity than a pgid
456	snapshot taken at one point in time — worth a look if a future reattach/process-matching bug turns out
457	to need sturdier identity than pgid gives. Not chasing a known bug today; this is "available primitive,
458	nobody has looked at it yet," filed so it isn't rediscovered from scratch.
459	
460	**Depends on:** nothing.
461	
462	**Priority:** P3 — no known bug this fixes today.
463	
464	### Re-benchmark surface-budget perf after the bump's upstream perf work (macapp) — filed 2026-08-14
465	
466	**What:** the 1.3.2 bump's ~1300 upstream commits (`332b2aef...35e1a016`) include a cluster of perf
467	work landing in the same window as the leak/crash fixes the bump's QA actually measured: scrollback
468	pages get LZ4-compressed once off-screen (`7e02af87`, upstream-reported "70-90% memory savings"),
469	render-state lock hold time cut (`98a7c0f6`), VT processing throughput increased (`634957c8`,
470	`2da015cd`), pty-read/parse pipelining added (`0535770e`, upstream-reported "+25-55% IO throughput"),
471	and occluded surfaces now skip `updateFrame` entirely (`14d9e600`). All five are confirmed ancestors of
472	our pinned `35e1a016` via the same compare range the bump's own QA walked. **None of this was in the
473	bump's QA scope** — `QA-libghostty-results/2026-08-12-libghostty-1.3.2-bump.md` measured leak
474	counts and small-N (10-20 pane) churn deltas, not throughput or memory-under-load at volume.
475	
476	**Why:** `QA-libghostty.md` §J ("Surface budget") already asks for exactly this measurement — open
477	50-100 tabs, watch CPU/GPU/memory, confirm occluded tabs idle — but it's an unchecked box with no
478	recorded baseline, not a measured "before" to diff against. This perf work is squarely what §J exists
479	to catch, and the bump shipped straight through it unmeasured.
480	
481	**How to start:** open 50-100 tabs across projects/workrooms (§J's own scale), record RSS/CPU/GPU via
482	Activity Monitor or `vmmap`, and specifically confirm a backgrounded/occluded tab's render cost drops
483	(switch away from an animating `htop` pane and watch its cost fall — §J's own check). There is no
484	existing 50-100 tab baseline to diff against on the old pin — record this as the first real number, not
485	a comparison.
486	
487	**Depends on:** nothing — can run today.
488	
489	**Priority:** P2 — a real, upstream-claimed perf win sitting completely unmeasured on a pin we already
490	shipped; worth confirming it landed for us, since it's the kind of thing surface-churn overhead could
491	also be masking either direction.
492	
493	### Own the GhosttyKit xcframework (macapp) — CMT-2, GA-time supply-chain decision

1700	### OSC 52 clipboard-confirmation policy (macapp)
1701	
1702	**What:** A real policy/UI for terminal-app clipboard access (OSC 52) — the runtime's
1703	`read_clipboard_cb` / `write_clipboard_cb`. Today writes are gated to `text/*` mime and reads use
1704	Ghostty's permissive default (auto-allow); `confirmReadClipboard` is a stub, so a deliberate
1705	prompt/allowlist is deferred.
1706	
1707	**Why:** Code-review finding #7. OSC 52 lets a remote program read/write the system pasteboard;
1708	the permissive default is fine for a beta (it matches Ghostty's own default) but a security-minded
1709	user should be able to require confirmation.
1710	
1711	**How to start:** Implement `confirm_read_clipboard_cb` to surface a prompt (or consult a
1712	`Defaults.Keys` policy: allow / prompt / deny); gate `write_clipboard_cb` similarly. Decide the
1713	default (Ghostty = allow).
1714	
1715	**Depends on:** the clipboard callbacks already wired
1716	(`macapp/WorkroomApp/Core/GhosttyRuntimeAdapter.swift`, `Core/GhosttyApp.swift`).
1717	
1718	**Priority:** P3 (permissive default is acceptable for the beta).
1719	
1720	### Quick-switcher deferrals (macapp) — #132 follow-ups
1721	
1722	**What:** Five things the ⌥Tab / ⌃Tab switcher shipped without, deliberately. Independent of each
1723	other; take them one at a time.
1724	
1725	- **MRU order in the ⌘O Open Workroom picker.** `SwitcherRecency` already answers "what did I use
1726	  last", so `OpenPickerModel` could rank by it instead of alphabetically. Cheap, but it reorders a
1727	  shipped, tested surface (`OpenPickerModelTests`) — hence deferred until we've lived with MRU in the
1728	  switcher and know it feels right there first.
1729	- **Scope ⌥Tab to the current Space.** A cross-window commit to a window on another Space animates the
1730	  Space switch for ~0.5–1s. Nothing is wrong, but it's a jarring result for a keystroke that reads as
1731	  instant. Either filter `QuickSwitcher.workroomSlots` by `hostWindow?.isOnActiveSpace` (and lose the
1732	  ability to reach those workrooms at all) or leave it; decide from use, not from taste.
1733	- **The shared `UnreadBadge` still draws the RAW accent.** The rail passes its own corrected pair
1734	  (`Palette.nsBadgeFill` == `nsRing`, ink measured), because a themed accent can sit close to the
1735	  surface it's on — the sidebar and toolbar badges have the same exposure and no correction. Now a
1736	  small change: `ThemeTokens.contrastRatio` is genuinely WCAG since `dfcc0bd8`, so
1737	  `legible(accent, on: host, target: 3.0)` at the component's own call sites means what it says.
1738	- **The 10s session ceiling cancels silently.** A stuck modifier can't leave the rail up forever, so
1739	  `QuickSwitcherReducer.sessionCeiling` ends the session — with **no commit**, so a user who held ⌥ for
1740	  eleven seconds while reading the rail gets nothing. Arguably the timeout should commit the cursor
1741	  instead. A product call, not a bug: pick one and say so in the reducer's doc comment.
1742	- **⌃-click on the pane rail is unverified.** ⌃-click is a secondary click, and the rail panel is never
1743	  key, so it may not deliver a `.onTapGesture` at all. Needs a **real mouse** — this repo has twice
1744	  been lied to by synthetic input (`macapp-textselection-swallows-taps`,
1745	  `macapp-hover-slide-release-only`), so an XCUITest pass here would prove nothing.
1746	
1747	**Why:** each of these was written down in the #132 plan's out-of-scope table and would otherwise be
1748	lost with it. Two other entries from that table are now **moot**: the window-capture layer was built
1749	and then removed (an aspect-fit terminal thumbnail at card size is a grey smudge that looks like every
1750	other terminal), so "a libghostty damage callback for thumbnail freshness" and "per-pane sensitive
1751	marking / screen-sharing auto-suppress" no longer have a subject — `Core/Snapshots/` is gone and the
1752	rail draws marks and miniatures instead.
1753	
1754	**Depends on:** nothing. The badge item wants `dfcc0bd8` (the contrast-metric fix), which has landed.
1755	
1756	**Priority:** P3 for all five.
1757	
1758	### Stream the inline terminal agent's diagnosis into the banner — #49 follow-up
1759	
1760	**What:** Show the diagnosis appearing live in the banner (claude `--output-format stream-json`)
1761	instead of a spinner during the (blocking) call.
1762	
1763	**Why:** Nicer perceived latency. Deferred deliberately, not dropped: (1) the diagnosis output is a

### OSC 52 clipboard-confirmation policy (macapp)

**What:** A real policy/UI for terminal-app clipboard access (OSC 52) — the runtime's
`read_clipboard_cb` / `write_clipboard_cb`. Today writes are gated to `text/*` mime and reads use
Ghostty's permissive default (auto-allow); `confirmReadClipboard` is a stub, so a deliberate
prompt/allowlist is deferred.

**Why:** Code-review finding #7. OSC 52 lets a remote program read/write the system pasteboard;
the permissive default is fine for a beta (it matches Ghostty's own default) but a security-minded
user should be able to require confirmation.

**How to start:** Implement `confirm_read_clipboard_cb` to surface a prompt (or consult a
`Defaults.Keys` policy: allow / prompt / deny); gate `write_clipboard_cb` similarly. Decide the
default (Ghostty = allow).

**Depends on:** the clipboard callbacks already wired
(`macapp/WorkroomApp/Core/GhosttyRuntimeAdapter.swift`, `Core/GhosttyApp.swift`).

**Priority:** P3 (permissive default is acceptable for the beta).

### Quick-switcher deferrals (macapp) — #132 follow-ups

**What:** Five things the ⌥Tab / ⌃Tab switcher shipped without, deliberately. Independent of each
other; take them one at a time.

- **MRU order in the ⌘O Open Workroom picker.** `SwitcherRecency` already answers "what did I use
  last", so `OpenPickerModel` could rank by it instead of alphabetically. Cheap, but it reorders a
  shipped, tested surface (`OpenPickerModelTests`) — hence deferred until we've lived with MRU in the
  switcher and know it feels right there first.
- **Scope ⌥Tab to the current Space.** A cross-window commit to a window on another Space animates the
  Space switch for ~0.5–1s. Nothing is wrong, but it's a jarring result for a keystroke that reads as
  instant. Either filter `QuickSwitcher.workroomSlots` by `hostWindow?.isOnActiveSpace` (and lose the
  ability to reach those workrooms at all) or leave it; decide from use, not from taste.
- **The shared `UnreadBadge` still draws the RAW accent.** The rail passes its own corrected pair
  (`Palette.nsBadgeFill` == `nsRing`, ink measured), because a themed accent can sit close to the
  surface it's on — the sidebar and toolbar badges have the same exposure and no correction. Now a
  small change: `ThemeTokens.contrastRatio` is genuinely WCAG since `dfcc0bd8`, so
  `legible(accent, on: host, target: 3.0)` at the component's own call sites means what it says.
- **The 10s session ceiling cancels silently.** A stuck modifier can't leave the rail up forever, so
  `QuickSwitcherReducer.sessionCeiling` ends the session — with **no commit**, so a user who held ⌥ for
  eleven seconds while reading the rail gets nothing. Arguably the timeout should commit the cursor
  instead. A product call, not a bug: pick one and say so in the reducer's doc comment.
- **⌃-click on the pane rail is unverified.** ⌃-click is a secondary click, and the rail panel is never
  key, so it may not deliver a `.onTapGesture` at all. Needs a **real mouse** — this repo has twice
  been lied to by synthetic input (`macapp-textselection-swallows-taps`,
  `macapp-hover-slide-release-only`), so an XCUITest pass here would prove nothing.

**Why:** each of these was written down in the #132 plan's out-of-scope table and would otherwise be
lost with it. Two other entries from that table are now **moot**: the window-capture layer was built
and then removed (an aspect-fit terminal thumbnail at card size is a grey smudge that looks like every
other terminal), so "a libghostty damage callback for thumbnail freshness" and "per-pane sensitive
marking / screen-sharing auto-suppress" no longer have a subject — `Core/Snapshots/` is gone and the
rail draws marks and miniatures instead.

**Depends on:** nothing. The badge item wants `dfcc0bd8` (the contrast-metric fix), which has landed.

**Priority:** P3 for all five.

### Stream the inline terminal agent's diagnosis into the banner — #49 follow-up

**What:** Show the diagnosis appearing live in the banner (claude `--output-format stream-json`)
instead of a spinner during the (blocking) call.

**Why:** Nicer perceived latency. Deferred deliberately, not dropped: (1) the diagnosis output is a
structured JSON object (`{summary, fix, detail}`) — that's what makes the "Insert fix" button
reliable (the on-demand eval validates it) — and streaming emits partial JSON deltas that don't
render nicely; (2) the inline diagnosis now runs on Haiku 4.5 (~2-3s), so the spinner is brief and
the payoff is marginal.

**How to start:** The clean approach that preserves the structured fix is to change the model's
output to "one-line prose summary, then a delimiter, then the JSON fix", stream the prose live while
parsing the JSON tail on completion. Needs: an incremental-stdout streaming runner (the current
`StatusCommandRunner` buffers to completion), a stream-json NDJSON delta parser, the split prompt +
parser, banner partial-text state, and its own entry in `AgentDiagnosisEvalTests`.

**Depends on:** the inline agent (#49, merged). Touches `AgentRunner`, `AgentPrompt`,
`TerminalAgentManager`, `TerminalAgentBanner`.

**Priority:** P3 (polish; marginal over a 2-3s spinner, and must not regress the structured fix).

## P3 — Inspector, window layout, and theming

### Back/forward doesn't reinstate the inspector section (macapp) — nav-history follow-up

**What:** `activeInspectorSection` is not part of a `NavLocation`, so ⌘[/⌘] never moves it. Add it to the
location and map content kinds to sections (`.diff`/`.file` → `.changes`, `.changeset` → the pane holding
History), suppressed under replay so it doesn't write the persisted default.

**Why:** narrower than it first looks, and worth stating so nobody re-scopes it wrongly:
`ActivitySection.changes` stacks `[.changes, .history, .pullRequest]` as sub-sections of **one** pane, so
moving between a diff and a commit needs no section switch at all — both lists are already on screen.
The only real case is **Files ↔ Changes**: open a file from the Files section, press Back to a diff, and
the pane is correct while the inspector still lists files, so no row highlights.

**How to start:** `AppStore.activeInspectorSection` (`@Published`, persisted in its `didSet`) plus the
`FocusedTabSelection` → `ActivitySection` mapping. `withHistorySuppressed` already exists for the
replay-side guard.

**Depends on:** nothing.

feat(macapp): rail thumbnails via own-window capture (issue #132, T12)

Real screenshots in the switcher rail. One window capture per shot, cropped into
N per-pane thumbnails, downscaled to the 72x56 well and cached.

No Screen Recording permission, no Info.plist key, no entitlement:
`SCShareableContent.currentProcess` returns content capturable "without user
consent via TCC", and the T1 spike confirmed the *capture* also hands back real
pixels — preflight false, no prompt, and a never-activated background window
captured fine. Verified again end-to-end here: a real terminal screenshot
renders in a card with no prompt.

The crop math is its own file with its own tests because the plan was wrong here
in two independent ways, both of which look obviously true:

    NSWindow.frame      (200, 200, 820, 552)   AppKit: y-UP,   bottom-left
    filter.contentRect  (205, 872, 810, 544)   CG:     y-DOWN, top-left, inset
    captured image       1620 x 1088  ==  contentRect x pointPixelScale, EXACTLY

`contentRect` is not the window frame — deriving the scale from the delivered
image against the frame gave 1.9756 (x) and 1.9710 (y), neither 2.0 nor equal to
each other, a ~1.2% drift that reaches ~10px by the far edge of a large window.
And the y-flips do not cancel, because `convertToScreen` is y-up while
`contentRect` is y-down. So the reference rect is always `contentRect`, the scale
is always `pointPixelScale`, and the region is flipped exactly once. The tests pin
the measured numbers: a fixture where `contentRect.size == frame.size` passes a
wrong implementation.

A mislabelled card is made structurally impossible rather than unlikely. The
epoch, the window frame and every region rect are read synchronously before the
await; if the epoch or the frame changed by the time pixels arrive, the whole
shot is discarded rather than cropped against new rects. Worst case is a stale
card, never a wrong one. A capture is also refused outright for a window that
isn't visible, is miniaturized, or is on another Space — that last one returns an
all-black *successful* image, which "keep the old entry on failure" would
cheerfully cache as the new truth.

Cache is LRU, bounded by count and bytes, with an injected clock, and treats an
older theme generation as a miss: the picture is of colours no longer on screen.
Correctness needs no purge-on-window-close hook, because `WindowToken` is a UUID
that is never reused, so a closed window's key cannot collide with a live one.

Designed degradation, now observed rather than assumed: only the selected
workroom has an on-screen region, so a workroom not visited this launch keeps its
glyph well, and the first-ever reveal shows glyphs because the capture lands after
the panel does.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

### A live "all terminals" mini-viewer — revisit, the old premise was wrong (macapp), filed 2026-08-14

**What:** re-examined the standing belief that a live dashboard of many running terminals ("show every
pane, with a detail view") isn't possible because libghostty doesn't support it. **That's not what
happened, and it's worth correcting in place rather than re-citing.** The only thing actually built and
shipped under #132 was OS-level capture (`8a1d2547`, "rail thumbnails via own-window capture") —
`SCShareableContent.currentProcess`, no TCC/permission, real pixels confirmed end-to-end. It was
**reverted** (`455d28e8`) and replaced by hue+monogram marks (`8de09cba`) for a UX reason — "an
aspect-fit terminal thumbnail at card size is a grey smudge that looks like every other terminal" — not
a technical block. **libghostty was never in that path at all**; the capture happened entirely at the
AppKit/ScreenCaptureKit layer, over the window's on-screen pixels.

**The real libghostty-side limitation is narrower, and still true on today's 1.3.2 pin (checked against
the currently-linked header, not assumed):** `GhosttyKit`'s apprt surface exposes no off-screen/headless
render API and no per-frame damage callback — `grep '^GHOSTTY_API'` on
`DerivedData/Build/Products/Debug/include/libghostty/ghostty.h` turns up exactly one draw-related
function, `ghostty_surface_draw` (ties to the view's own bound Metal layer — not a
render-to-buffer-regardless-of-visibility call), no bitmap/texture/screenshot function, no cursor-position
query, and no cell/grid/color inspection API of any kind. This is the same gap CMT-3's accessibility
entry already names ("no render/damage callback... checked before building this",
`GhosttySurfaceView.swift:984-989`) — it's real, just not what killed #132.

**What IS available today that wasn't the thing evaluated last time:**
`ghostty_surface_read_text(surface, GHOSTTY_POINT_VIEWPORT, …)` — already wired for the a11y poll
(`GhosttySurfaceView.swift:1002-1008`) — reads a surface's live VT-state text directly, **with no
dependency on the surface's window being on-screen at all**. That's the opposite constraint from the
capture approach: `ghostty_surface_set_occlusion` (`GhosttySurfaceView.swift:540`) only gates the
render/GPU path (the mechanism behind the bump's `updateFrame`-skip perf win — see the
surface-budget-rebenchmark entry above), while `ghostty_app_tick` (`GhosttyApp.swift:251`) pumps every
surface's IO/VT-state unconditionally — which is also why title/OSC-9-notification/bell all keep
working for backgrounded tabs today. So a preview built on `read_text` should stay live for a pane in a
workroom that isn't even the frontmost window, not just one that's occluded-but-open. **Not yet proven
empirically for this exact call** — the one-line check is: pipe fresh output into an occluded/背景
surface, call `read_text` immediately after, confirm the content reflects it.

**The catch:** `ghostty_text_s` is `{ const char* text; uintptr_t text_len; }` — plain bytes, no
color/attribute/cursor-position data (checked the struct directly). A `read_text`-based mini-viewer is a
live monochrome text peek (closer to `tail -f` than a real terminal render) — legitimate for "what's this
pane doing right now," not a faithful miniature of the real terminal.

**A real colored live render is a bigger, separately-scoped bet:** this cycle's upstream digest
surfaced a brand-new **`libghostty-vt`** library — distinct from `GhosttyKit`, its own
xcframework/packaging, not currently linked by us — that adds exactly the missing pieces: grid/cell
inspection with color (`d2a29de9`, `df8813bf`, `5c8b9f3f`), a render-state API (cursor, colors, dirty
rows: `00ffc22e` + ~15 follow-ups), and `total_rows`/`scrollback_rows` getters (`f452087e`). That's the
path to a real colored dashboard without OS capture — but it's a second dependency to vendor and link
alongside `GhosttyKit`, not a header away.

**How to start, smallest-first:**
1. Confirm `read_text` stays live on an occluded/background surface (the one-line check above).
2. A monochrome text-peek mini-viewer using the already-wired `read_text` call — no new libghostty
   dependency, works for any live surface regardless of which window is frontmost. This is the
   part that's newly concrete since #132: it wasn't the thing evaluated, and it doesn't share
   window-capture's "must be on-screen" constraint.
3. If a colored render is wanted later, that's the `libghostty-vt` integration — track separately, and
   don't block (2) on it.

**Depends on:** nothing for step 1/2. Step 3 depends on a deliberate decision to add a second libghostty
dependency (same supply-chain question as "Own the GhosttyKit xcframework," CMT-2, above).

**Priority:** P3 — no user complaint driving this; filed so the next person doesn't re-derive "we looked
into this, wasn't possible" from a premise that was never quite right.

content.text:
Dug into the actual embedding contract instead of guessing. Found something better than either prior idea: **the real panes already live simultaneously in memory today** — no capture, no new dependency needed.

## 1. Reparent the real live surfaces into a grid (strongest option)

`TerminalTab.surface: GhosttySurfaceView?` (`TerminalSessions.swift:34`) — **every open tab keeps its real `GhosttySurfaceView` alive persistently**, focused or not, workroom-frontmost or not. Splits already prove N simultaneously-rendering panes works today (`activityPulses`' "visible but non-focused" case, `TerminalSessions.swift`) — a dashboard grid is just that, extended across workrooms instead of confined to one split-tree.

Per-surface runtime shrink already has confirmed API support, some already used elsewhere in the code:
- `ghostty_surface_update_config` (font-size, per-surface) — the exact method `GhosttySurfaceView.swift:625` already calls for theme reload
- `ghostty_surface_set_content_scale(surface, x, y)` — per-surface DPI
- `ghostty_surface_set_size(surface, w, h)` — per-surface pixel/column resize

So: reparent a tab's real NSView into a dashboard tile, shrink font-size + size via the above, un-occlude it. **Real color, real cursor, real everything, crisp at small size** — because it's actually rendering small, not a downscaled screenshot smudge (the exact defect that killed #132's capture approach). Restore to normal tab on exit.

Cost, stated plainly: un-occluding N tiles reintroduces the per-frame GPU cost the occlusion-skip optimization exists to avoid. Mitigate by virtualizing — only tiles actually in the dashboard's on-screen scroll viewport get un-occluded, same idle-when-off-screen pattern tabs already use. Engineering risk: this codebase has known NSView-remount sharp edges (the `isTornDown` guard exists because of exactly this class of bug) — reparenting needs care, but it's an AppKit lifecycle problem, not a libghostty one.

## 2. Always-on mirror window + reuse T12's ScreenCaptureKit code (fallback)

Give each pane its own tiny perpetual auxiliary window, force `ghostty_surface_set_occlusion(surface, true)` always so it keeps actually rendering regardless of which workroom is frontmost, capture on demand via SCK (T12's crop/cache/scale math already exists in git history, just reverted). Real live pixels, zero new libghostty API. Same GPU tax as #1, plus extra windows — and only fixes the blur if the tile is shown large enough to read, same lesson as #1. Weaker than #1 since it solves nothing #1 doesn't, at more complexity.

## 3. libghostty-vt, revisited (if you want zero GPU duplication)

The new upstream cell/grid/color API (not linked today) would let you paint your own cheap CPU preview (SwiftUI Canvas) from live cell data — true live, true color, no second Metal surface. Real dependency-vendoring work, separate track.

**My call: #1.** It's not a new capability, it's wiring together things that already exist (persistent surfaces + per-surface config API), and it directly fixes the reason the old attempt got reverted.

content.text:
No. Real, concrete reasons, not hedging:

**Resize = real reflow, not a shrink.** `ghostty_surface_set_size` changes pixel dimensions, which recomputes columns/rows (from cell size). Fewer columns → the engine reflows text and — for any TUI (vim, htop, tmux, an agent CLI) — triggers a real resize event the program redraws for. This is already confirmed, existing behavior in this exact engine: `QA-libghostty.md:18-19` — "Run a full-screen TUI → resize the window → reflows cleanly." Shrinking a pane into a tile fires that same path. The mini view wouldn't show a miniature of what's on the full pane right now — it'd show that same shell/process re-rendered for a *different* terminal geometry. Different wrap points, different TUI layout, possibly a different visible slice of output entirely.

**Real side effect, not cosmetic.** A resize sends a real signal (SIGWINCH-class) to the foreground process. A progress bar, a `less`, a build script formatting output to terminal width — all can visibly reflow/redraw/glitch from being resized into the tile and back out again on every dashboard open/close.

**One workaround, but it doesn't help:** shrink font-size in lockstep with pixel size to keep columns/rows *constant* (true zoom-out, no reflow, no SIGWINCH — genuinely identical content). But do the math on typical dashboard-tile size vs. an 80×24 pane: the font lands around 2-3pt. Identical data, illegible — defeats the point of a glanceable mini view.

**Structural, not just visual:** it's the same live `NSView`/surface instance moved, not a copy. It can be in the dashboard tile *or* its normal tab, never both at once. If part of the ask is "see the mini view of pane X while I'm also working in pane X full-size elsewhere," reparenting categorically can't do that — only a pixel-capture mirror or a separate CPU-drawn preview (libghostty-vt) can, since those don't touch the real surface's geometry or exclusivity at all.

**Net:** reparent-and-shrink is real, live, colored — but it's an honestly-different render of the same session, with a real disruption cost, and it's exclusive-use, not simultaneous. If "identical to the full pane, viewable alongside it" is the actual requirement, the capture-based mirror (idea #2) is the better fit despite being more machinery — it never touches the real pane's geometry, so it's pixel-faithful by construction.

content.text:
Right — that's the constraint I should've centered on immediately. Correcting.

**Drop the reparent/resize idea. Use continuous capture instead — content never touches the real surface's geometry.**

`ScreenCaptureKit` has two capture modes, and #132/T12 only used the weaker one:

- **One-shot** (`SCShareableContent.currentProcess` + screenshot) — what T12 built. Poll-based, single frame per call.
- **`SCStream`** (continuous) — a persistent stream that pushes fresh frames as the source changes, and you set the **output** width/height in `SCStreamConfiguration` independent of the source's actual point size. The compositor scales server-side. This is the same mechanism screen-sharing apps use.

Why this fits what you actually asked for:
- **Identical, not resized** — the source pane's real `ghostty_surface_t` geometry is never touched. No `set_size`, no font change, no reflow, no SIGWINCH to whatever's running in it. What you're capturing is the exact same columns/rows/content as the full pane, always.
- **Genuinely live** — continuous push per frame, not a manual re-poll loop.
- **Coexists with the full pane** — since this captures compositor pixels, not the `NSView` object itself, the same pane can be full-size in its tab **and** live in a dashboard tile simultaneously. No exclusivity problem like the reparent idea had.

One real constraint carries over, and it's physical, not a technique flaw: **the source still has to actually be rendering somewhere on-screen for there to be pixels to capture.** A backgrounded tab that libghostty has occluded (or a view AppKit isn't compositing at all) has nothing to stream. So this still needs every pane you want mirrored to be un-occluded and mounted — same GPU cost as before, unavoidable no matter which capture mechanism moves the pixels. `SCStream` just makes the delivery continuous and correctly-scaled instead of manually re-polling a screenshot.

One thing I haven't verified and won't claim: whether `SCStream`'s own-process capture is gated the same permission-free way the one-shot path was proven to be (memory: `sck-own-process-capture-no-tcc.md` only confirmed the screenshot API, not the streaming one). That's a fast, concrete check before committing to this — a few lines of test code, not a research project.

Before running anything that controls or drives the machine — XCUITest runs (`make app-uitest`, a
scoped `xcodebuild test` on a UI scheme), launching/quitting the app, System Events or `osascript`
automation, `screencapture`, synthetic CGEvent clicks/keystrokes — **ask first and wait**. Doing the
non-driving work (edits, `make app-format`, `make app-lint`, `make app-build`) up front and then
asking once for a single uninterrupted window is the shape Joel accepted.

**Why:** Joel is often using the machine at the same time. Driving it unannounced either surprises
them mid-task or makes the run itself fail, because a stolen keystroke lands in whatever they were
actually doing.

**How to apply:** batch everything that needs the machine into one permission request rather than
asking per command. Say what will be driven and roughly how long (e.g. "6 XCUITest cases, ~50s of
typing and clicking"). Unit suites (`make app-test`) also launch the app host, so include them in
the ask even though they don't hijack input. Related: [[macapp-visual-qa]],
[[macapp-uitest-only-relevant-class]], [[macapp-xcuitest-automation-wedge]].

18	/// panes can be visible at once; this view's mount/dismantle is the per-mount backstop.

21	/// on-screen layout via the recursive pane renderer over `PaneLayout` — splitting does not nest
22	/// surfaces inside a tab.
23	///
24	/// Focus (issue #3): with multiple panes mounted, only the focused one may grab first responder.
25	/// `isFocusedPane` drives that — the host passes `true` for exactly the focused leaf. Mount no longer
26	/// force-focuses unconditionally (that would let the last-mounted pane steal focus); focus is applied
27	/// from `isFocusedPane` on update. A pane the user clicks becomes first responder via the surface's own
28	/// `mouseDown`, which feeds the selection back through `onFocused`.
29	struct TerminalContainerView: NSViewRepresentable {
30	  let view: GhosttySurfaceView
31	  /// Whether this pane should hold keyboard focus. Solo callers leave it `true`; the split renderer
32	  /// passes `true` only for the focused leaf.
33	  var isFocusedPane: Bool = true
34	  /// When a status bar is stacked below the surface (issue #49), the surface rounds only its TOP
35	  /// corners so the terminal and the bar together read as one rounded panel (the enclosing clip
36	  /// rounds the bottom). Solo/default keeps all four rounded.
37	  var roundsBottomCorners: Bool = true
38	
39	  func makeNSView(context: Context) -> NSView {
40	    let container = NSView()
41	    container.wantsLayer = true
42	    // Round the terminal's corners. masksToBounds clips the hosted surface (pinned to the
43	    // container edges) to the rounded shape.
44	    container.layer?.cornerRadius = TerminalPanelMetrics.cornerRadius
45	    container.layer?.cornerCurve = .continuous
46	    container.layer?.masksToBounds = true
47	    applyRoundedCorners(container)
48	    mount(in: container)
49	    applyFocus(in: container)
50	    return container
51	  }

54	    applyRoundedCorners(container)
55	    mount(in: container)
56	    applyFocus(in: container)
57	  }

60	    container.layer?.maskedCorners =
61	      roundsBottomCorners

### A live "all terminals" mini-viewer — revisit, the old premise was wrong (macapp), filed 2026-08-14

**What:** re-examined the standing belief that a live dashboard of many running terminals ("show every
pane, with a detail view") isn't possible because libghostty doesn't support it. **That's not what
happened, and it's worth correcting in place rather than re-citing.** The only thing actually built and
shipped under #132 was OS-level capture (`8a1d2547`, "rail thumbnails via own-window capture") —
`SCShareableContent.currentProcess`, no TCC/permission, real pixels confirmed end-to-end. It was
**reverted** (`455d28e8`) and replaced by hue+monogram marks (`8de09cba`) for a UX reason — "an
aspect-fit terminal thumbnail at card size is a grey smudge that looks like every other terminal" — not
a technical block. **libghostty was never in that path at all**; the capture happened entirely at the
AppKit/ScreenCaptureKit layer, over the window's on-screen pixels.

**Hard requirement (stated explicitly, 2026-08-14): the mini view must be identical to the full pane,
not a resized/reflowed one.** Ruled out on that basis: shrinking a pane by calling
`ghostty_surface_set_size`/reducing font-size recomputes columns/rows, which reflows text and sends a
real resize signal to whatever's running in the pane (confirmed existing behavior at this pin —
`QA-libghostty.md:18-19`, "resize the window → reflows cleanly"). That's a different render of the same
session, not a miniature of the current one, and it's structurally exclusive with the real pane (same
NSView, one superview at a time — can't show both at once). Ruled out for that reason, not revisited
below.

**Validated path: a continuous `SCStream`, not the one-shot capture #132 used.**
`ScreenCaptureKit` has two capture modes; #132/T12 only used the weaker one (`SCScreenshotManager`,

window pauses via `viewDidMoveToWindow`" — confirms a tab that is **not** the currently-displayed one in
its strip has its `GhosttySurfaceView` fully detached from any window (`mount(in:)` at
`TerminalContainerView.swift:82-83` explicitly detaches whatever was shown when a different tab is
selected — "do NOT tear down — it lives on in the cache"). So for any tab that isn't already visible
(the common case for a hover-preview), there is nothing on-screen for `SCStream` to capture *until* it's
briefly re-mounted somewhere. The surface object itself is never destroyed — `TerminalTab.surface`
(`TerminalSessions.swift:34`) holds it regardless of focus — so there's always something to re-home,
never something to recreate.

1. Debounce the hover (~150-200ms hover-intent delay, same shape as any tab-preview UX) before doing
   anything — avoids mount/stream churn on a fast mouse sweep across several chips.
2. Re-home the hovered tab's `GhosttySurfaceView` into a small preview-host container, reusing the exact
   re-parenting mechanism `mount(in:)` already uses for split↔solo transitions (frame + autoresizing

   measured: cold re-mount-to-first-frame latency.** The `SCStream` check above only proved streaming
   works against an already-warm, already-visible window — it says nothing about how long a
   just-unoccluded surface takes to produce its first composited frame. Spike and measure this before
   any UI polish; if it's hundreds of ms the preview will feel sluggish and may need a skeleton/fade-in.

   rediscovering the same race here.

Repo: /Users/joelmoss/dev/workroom (macOS SwiftUI app under macapp/WorkroomApp). I'm planning a "hover a terminal tab chip to show a small live preview" feature, built on ScreenCaptureKit's continuous `SCStream` (already validated separately — own-process capture needs no Screen Recording permission). The preview needs to briefly re-mount and un-occlude a BACKGROUND tab's real `GhosttySurfaceView` (which is normally fully detached from any window when not the active tab), capture a few live frames of it via SCStream, then detach it again — all without it ever gaining keyboard focus.

Find and report back (file paths + line numbers, quote relevant code):

1. `GhosttySurfaceView.swift` — read the full occlusion mechanism: `setVisible`, `applyOcclusionState`, `isPaneVisible`, `isWindowVisible`, `updateWindowVisibility`, and `viewDidMoveToWindow` (or equivalent lifecycle methods). Exactly what happens when a surface is un-occluded after being occluded — is there any warm-up delay, any async work, anything that would affect how quickly a first frame appears after `setVisible(true)`? Also report `createSurface` — does mounting an ALREADY-CREATED surface (one whose `ghostty_surface_t` already exists) into a new container do any different work than a first-time mount (`pendingSurfaceCreation` path)?

2. Does `GhosttySurfaceView` own or bind to a `CAMetalLayer` directly (search for `CAMetalLayer`, `wantsLayer`, `makeBackingLayer`, `layer(for:)`)? Report exactly how the view's layer is set up — this matters for confirming a `SCStream`/`SCContentFilter` against the app's real window would actually see this surface's rendered content once mounted+visible.

3. `TerminalSessions.swift` — how does the model track which tab(s) are CURRENTLY on-screen/visible for a given `TerminalTarget` right now (splits show multiple simultaneously; a plain tab strip shows one)? Look for `focusedTabByTarget`, `splitByTarget`, `displayedTabIDs`, `reconcileOcclusion` (mentioned in a doc comment elsewhere) or similar. I need to know how to determine, given an arbitrary tab a user is hovering, whether it is ALREADY visible (so a hover-preview can skip re-mounting) or is a background tab (needs re-homing).

4. Search for any existing `.task(id:)` cancellation-related code or a generation-counter pattern used elsewhere in this codebase for "cancel the previous in-flight thing when a new one starts" (e.g. search bar debouncing, quick-switcher session state, hover/hold timers). Report the pattern used and its file:line, since a hover-preview will need the same shape (cancel a previous hover's mount+stream when the user moves to a different tab quickly).

This is read-only research for a plan — do not propose implementation, just report what exists with exact file:line citations and short code quotes. Keep the report organized by the four numbered items above.

<result># Report: Hover-preview feature research

## 1. `TerminalTabStrip.swift` — chip construction & existing hover/tooltip/identity

File: `/Users/joelmoss/dev/workroom/macapp/WorkroomApp/Views/TerminalTabStrip.swift`

**Chip is built in two layers.** `TerminalTabStrip.chipRun` (lines 122–245) iterates `tabs` in a `ForEach` and wraps each `TerminalTabChip` (a private, purely-presentational view, lines 467–657) with all the interactive modifiers — hover, tap, drag, context menu. The chip view itself takes no live model reference, only value/closure params (`tab: TerminalTab`, `isActive`, `isHovered`, etc.) — comment at line 465: "Purely presentational — the strip wraps it with the hover, tap, and drag gestures, since those drive (and read) the strip's shared drag state."

**Hover already exists**, driven from the strip, not the chip:
```swift
// TerminalTabStrip.swift:168-170
.onHover { inside in
  if inside { hoveredTab = tab.id } else if hoveredTab == tab.id { hoveredTab = nil }
}
```
`hoveredTab: TerminalTab.ID?` (line 40) is single-selection strip state — only one chip can be "hovered" at a time, and it's used purely for the visual wash (`isHovered` passed to `TerminalTabChip`) and to suppress adjacent dividers (`showsLeadingSeparator`, line 395). There is no hover-driven overlay/preview UI on chips today, and no delay — it's an instant boolean flip, same idiom used everywhere else in the codebase (see §4).

**`.help()` tooltip already present**, on the *chip*, not per-element:
```swift
// TerminalTabStrip.swift:648
.help(tab.filePath ?? tab.title)
```
This shows the full untruncated title/path after macOS's standard tooltip delay. A hover-preview feature would compete for the same hover gesture/region as this tooltip (both fire from the same `.onHover`-tracked region — SwiftUI's `.help` installs its own AppKit tracking area).

**Accessibility identifier scheme — note the mismatch with your assumption.** The chip's identifier is `terminal.tab.<title>`, **not** `workroom.tab.*`:
```swift
// TerminalTabStrip.swift:649
.accessibilityIdentifier("terminal.tab.\(tab.title)")
```
(`workroom.pane.close` at line 851 is a different, unrelated control — the "remove from split" button in the pane title bar. `WorkroomTabBar.swift` — the sibling *workroom*-level tab bar, not the terminal-tab strip — presumably has its own `workroom.tab.*` scheme; I did not find one in this file.)

**What data the chip has access to:**
- `tab: TerminalTab` (full value, `TerminalSessions.swift:15`), including:
  - `tab.surface: GhosttySurfaceView?` (`TerminalSessions.swift:34-37`) — nil for non-terminal (diff/file/changeset) tabs; `GhosttySurfaceView` is `final class GhosttySurfaceView: NSView` (`GhosttySurfaceView.swift:17`), i.e. the actual live Metal-backed AppKit view for that tab's terminal — reachable straight off the chip's own `tab` binding, no lookup needed.
  - `tab.title`, `tab.filePath` (repo-relative path for diff/file tabs), `tab.isPreview`, `tab.isRunning`, `tab.content` (enum `.terminal/.diff/.file/.changeset`).
  - Already used elsewhere off the same `tab`: `tab.surface?.sendText(fix)` (`TerminalTabStrip.swift:446`, inside the agent popover), so "reach the live surface from a tab-strip-adjacent view" is an established pattern.
- **No frame/position data today.** Each chip's *width* is captured via a `PreferenceKey` (`TabWidthKey`, lines 660-667) fed by a `GeometryReader` background (lines 606-610) — used only for the drag-reorder math (`widths: [TerminalTab.ID: CGFloat]`, line 51). There is no per-chip *global frame/anchor* captured anywhere in this file — you'd need to add that (e.g. an `Anchor<CGRect>` preference or a second `GeometryReader` reading `.global`) to position a hover preview under a specific chip.

## 2. Existing floating/anchored overlay UI

Three genuinely different mechanisms exist in this codebase; none of them is a generic "hover preview" but each is a real precedent for a different piece of the puzzle.

### a) `TerminalSearchBar.swift` — pure SwiftUI `.overlay`, no separate window
File: `/Users/joelmoss/dev/workroom/macapp/WorkroomApp/Views/TerminalSearchBar.swift`, mounted at `/Users/joelmoss/dev/workroom/macapp/WorkroomApp/Views/PaneTreeView.swift:496-502`:
```swift
// PaneTreeView.swift:496-502
// Scrollback find bar (⌘F), pinned top-trailing over the focused pane only — search state
// is per-surface, and only the focused pane can be searched. Nothing until active.
.overlay(alignment: .topTrailing) {
  if focused {
    TerminalSearchBar(model: s.view.searchModel)
  }
}
```
- **Mechanism:** a plain SwiftUI `.overlay(alignment:)` directly on `TerminalContainerView` (the `NSViewRepresentable` hosting the terminal surface) — it lives in the same view hierarchy, above the AppKit-hosted surface, not a separate window/panel.
- **Positioning:** `alignment: .topTrailing` on the overlay + the bar's own `.padding(10)` (`TerminalSearchBar.swift:71`) — no measured frame math, just corner-alignment + fixed inset.
- **Shown/dismissed:** conditional on `focused` (SwiftUI `if`, so it mounts/unmounts) and `model.isActive` (an `@ObservedObject` model's published flag) — driven by ⌘F, not hover. Dismissed via `model.end()` from an explicit close button or `.onExitCommand` (Esc), `TerminalSearchBar.swift:82`.
- **Focus interplay is notable and load-bearing** for anything else that wants to sit over a terminal: `TerminalContainerView.applyFocus` (`TerminalContainerView.swift:118-119`) explicitly yields to the search bar (`if view.searchModel.isActive { return }`) so it doesn't steal first-responder back from the field. A hover preview overlay wouldn't need first-responder, but it's the concrete example of "a SwiftUI overlay sitting on top of the Metal surface" already existing and being hit-testable (SwiftUI overlay content over an `NSViewRepresentable` does receive clicks/hover — confirmed by this bar's own buttons working).

### b) `SwitcherRailView.swift` / `SwitcherPanel.swift` — dedicated non-activating `NSPanel`
Files: `/Users/joelmoss/dev/workroom/macapp/WorkroomApp/Views/SwitcherRailView.swift`, `/Users/joelmoss/dev/workroom/macapp/WorkroomApp/Core/SwitcherPanel.swift`.
- **Mechanism:** a real second window — the app's first `NSPanel` (comment at `SwitcherPanel.swift:4`):
```swift
// SwitcherPanel.swift:10-15
final class SwitcherPanel: NSPanel {
  override var canBecomeKey: Bool { false }
  override var canBecomeMain: Bool { false }
}
```
Built once and reused (`SwitcherPanelController.prepare()`, `SwitcherPanel.swift:43-77`): `styleMask: [.nonactivatingPanel, .borderless]`, `isFloatingPanel = true`, `level = .floating`, `isOpaque = false`, `hasShadow = false` (the rail draws its own shadow in SwiftUI — see `SwitcherRailView.swift:207-240` — because a borderless non-opaque `NSPanel` was measured to cast **no** system shadow at all, comment at `SwitcherRailView.swift:213`), `isReleasedWhenClosed = false`. Content is an `NSHostingView(rootView: SwitcherRailView(model: model))`.
- **Positioning:** computed per-reveal in `SwitcherPanelController.show(items:cursor:)` (`SwitcherPanel.swift:105-126`) — sized by `SwitcherRailLayout.panelSize(count:visibleFrame:)` and positioned by `SwitcherRailLayout.panelOrigin(size:windowFrame:visibleFrame:)`, i.e. computed against the **key window's frame** and the screen's `visibleFrame`, not a measured SwiftUI anchor.
- **Shown/dismissed:** `panel.orderFrontRegardless()` / `panel.orderOut(nil)` (`SwitcherPanel.swift:125,129`) — driven by the ⌥Tab/⌃Tab controller (`QuickSwitcherController`), keystroke-driven, not hover. Critically it **never becomes key** (`canBecomeKey/canBecomeMain` overridden false) so the workroom window keeps first responder/key status the whole time it's shown — the comment stresses this is load-bearing for the release-detection gesture.
- Card-level hover *inside* the rail is the plain instant idiom (`SwitcherRailView.swift:276`): `.onHover { inside in if inside { model.onHover?(index) } }`, routed back through the controller (not straight to state) specifically because of a movement-threshold guard (comment at `SwitcherPanel.swift:92-93`): "Hover goes through the controller, not straight to the model: the D17 movement threshold lives there, so a card hovered because the panel opened under a stationary pointer is discarded." — worth knowing if a hover-preview's reveal shouldn't fire just because the pointer happened to already be over a chip when something else redraws.

### c) `NSPopover` usage (two more precedents, neither in your named files)
- `MenuBarController.swift:20-45` — a hand-hosted `NSPopover` anchored to the status-bar item's `NSStatusItem.button`, `behavior = .transient` (closes on click-away), shown on click (`handleClick` action), content is `NSHostingController(rootView: MenuBarNotificationsView(...))`.
- SwiftUI's own `.popover` modifier (anchored to the *attaching view*, not a manually-positioned window) is used twice already, both **click**-triggered, not hover:
  - `TerminalTabStrip.swift:161-167` — the ✦ agent-diagnosis popover, `.popover(isPresented: Binding(get: { agentPopoverTab == tab.id }, ...))` attached directly to the chip.
  - `TerminalStatusBar.swift:172-175` — the agent-usage quota detail, `.popover(isPresented: usageDetailPresented, arrowEdge: .bottom) { AgentUsageDetailView(...) }`.

### d) The closest existing analogue to "hover to reveal a small preview": `TerminalStatusBar.swift`'s delayed-hover popover
This is the single best precedent for your feature — same shape (hover a small chip → after a short delay, show more detail in a floating panel → hide on exit), already shipped:
```swift
// TerminalStatusBar.swift:34-42
@State private var usageDetailHovering = false
@State private var usageHoverRevealWorkItem: DispatchWorkItem?
...
private let usageHoverRevealDelay: TimeInterval = 0.4

// TerminalStatusBar.swift:162-171
.onHover { hovering in
  usageHoverRevealWorkItem?.cancel()
  if hovering {
    let workItem = DispatchWorkItem { usageDetailHovering = true }
    usageHoverRevealWorkItem = workItem
    DispatchQueue.main.asyncAfter(deadline: .now() + usageHoverRevealDelay, execute: workItem)
  } else {
    usageDetailHovering = false
  }
}
.popover(isPresented: usageDetailPresented, arrowEdge: .bottom) {
  AgentUsageDetailView(snapshot: snapshot, now: Date())
    .frame(width: AgentUsageDetailView.popoverWidth)
}
```
Key details: exit is instant (no symmetric delay on hide — `usageDetailHovering = false` immediately), the delay is only on *reveal* (arm-and-cancel via `DispatchWorkItem`, cancelled on every hover-state change so a quick pass-through never fires it), and it composes with a separate "pinned" boolean (`usageDetailPinned`, set by click) via a combined `Binding` (`usageDetailPresented`, lines 123-132) so click-to-pin and hover-to-peek share one popover without fighting each other. Comment at lines 31-33 states the intent plainly: "Set after a short hover delay ..., so a mouse merely passing over the segment doesn't pop a popover; cleared the instant the mouse leaves."

## 3. `TerminalContainerView.swift` — full file read

File: `/Users/joelmoss/dev/workroom/macapp/WorkroomApp/Views/TerminalContainerView.swift` (129 lines, read in full above).

**Surface-frame/container relationship:**
- The container is a bare `NSView` created in `makeNSView` (line 40), `wantsLayer = true`, corner-radius/clip applied via `container.layer` (lines 44-46) — not an `NSView` subclass with any custom logic beyond that.
- The surface (`view: GhosttySurfaceView`) is pinned to the container purely via **frame + autoresizing mask**, deliberately **not** AutoLayout constraints:
```swift
// TerminalContainerView.swift:90-93
view.translatesAutoresizingMaskIntoConstraints = true
view.frame = container.bounds
view.autoresizingMask = [.width, .height]
container.addSubview(view)
```
The comment (lines 85-89) explains why: a surface is re-homed between containers (split ⟷ solo) while the old container may still be alive mid-transition, and lingering AutoLayout constraints to a stale container previously left the surface at a broken/zero frame (a blank pane, issue #3). So **the surface's frame always == its current container's bounds**, kept in sync automatically by the autoresizing mask on every container resize — there's no independent sizing of the surface from its container today.

Repo: /Users/joelmoss/dev/workroom, macOS SwiftUI app under macapp/WorkroomApp. Design a concrete implementation plan for a new feature: hovering a terminal tab chip shows a small, genuinely LIVE, pixel-identical preview of that tab's terminal content (not a resized/reflowed re-render — the real pane's geometry must never change).

## Why "identical, not resized" is a hard constraint
Already explored and rejected: shrinking the pane via `ghostty_surface_set_size`/font-size changes columns/rows, which reflows text and sends a real resize signal to whatever's running in the pane (confirmed existing behavior in this app: `QA-libghostty.md:18-19`, "resize the window → reflows cleanly"). That's a different render of the same session, not a miniature of the current one. So the preview must be produced by capturing the real, unmodified surface's actual rendered pixels.

## Validated capture mechanism (already empirically confirmed, not theoretical)
Continuous `ScreenCaptureKit` `SCStream` against `SCShareableContent.currentProcess` (own-process content) needs **no Screen Recording permission** — confirmed today via a standalone compiled Swift binary that opened a real NSWindow, built `SCContentFilter(desktopIndependentWindow:)`, and ran a real `SCStream`: 31 frames delivered over 3 seconds at the configured `minimumFrameInterval` (1/10s), exit 0, no TCC prompt, no permission error. `SCStreamConfiguration.width/height` scales output independently of the source's real point size — so the preview's pixel size is controlled at the stream-config level, never by touching the terminal's own geometry.

There is a real, physical constraint that doesn't go away: the source surface must actually be rendering and mounted on-screen for there to be anything to capture. A backgrounded (non-selected) tab's surface is fully detached from any window today (confirmed, see below) — nothing to capture until it's briefly re-mounted and un-occluded for the hover's duration.

## Confirmed architecture facts (from two research passes just completed — trust these, they are read from the actual current code, not assumed)

**Tab chip / hover UI** (`Views/TerminalTabStrip.swift`):
- Chips built by `TerminalTabChip` (lines 467-657, purely presentational — takes `tab: TerminalTab` + closures, no live model lookup needed since `tab.surface: GhosttySurfaceView?` is right there on the value).
- Hover already tracked at the strip level: `.onHover { inside in ... hoveredTab = tab.id ... }` (lines 168-170) — single-selection, instant, no delay. A `.help()` tooltip already fires off the same hover region (line 648) — will compete for attention with a new preview.
- **No per-chip frame/anchor is captured today** — only chip *width* via a `PreferenceKey` (`TabWidthKey`, lines 660-667) for drag-reorder math. A hover preview needs to add its own anchor capture (e.g. `Anchor<CGRect>` preference, same idiom already used for `TabWidthKey`) to position itself under the hovered chip.
- Accessibility id is `terminal.tab.<title>` (line 649) — correcting an earlier assumption of `workroom.tab.*`, which is a different, unrelated control.

**Closest existing precedent — copy this shape** (`Views/TerminalStatusBar.swift:34-42, 162-171`): a 0.4s hover-reveal delay via `DispatchWorkItem` + `asyncAfter`, cancelled/re-armed on every hover-state flip, instant hide, feeding a `.popover(isPresented:arrowEdge:)` that also composes with a click-to-pin boolean via a combined `Binding`. This is the established "hover a small chip → after a beat → show more detail in a floating view" idiom in this codebase — reuse it rather than inventing a new hover-dwell mechanism.

Secondary precedents worth knowing:
- `Views/HistoryPanel.swift:380-391` — a `.task(id: hovering)` dwell-then-reveal (500ms sleep, `Task.isCancelled` check) — an alternative dwell shape, SwiftUI-native.
- `Views/EdgeRevealSidebar.swift` — instant reveal, DEBOUNCED hide (180ms, re-checks "still idle" before committing) — relevant if the preview panel itself needs to survive the cursor moving from the chip onto the preview.
- `Views/TerminalSearchBar.swift` + `Views/PaneTreeView.swift:496-502` — precedent for a plain SwiftUI `.overlay(alignment:)` sitting directly on top of the AppKit-hosted terminal surface (no separate window needed) — one viable way to host the preview, vs. `Core/SwitcherPanel.swift`'s heavier non-activating `NSPanel` approach (`canBecomeKey/canBecomeMain` overridden false, floats above without stealing key window — used for the ⌥Tab switcher rail).

**Occlusion + mount mechanics** (`Core/GhosttySurfaceView.swift`, `Views/TerminalContainerView.swift`):
- `setVisible(_:)` → `applyOcclusionState()` → `ghostty_surface_set_occlusion(surface, isPaneVisible && isWindowVisible)` (lines ~525-541) is **fully synchronous, zero artificial delay** on the Swift side. Any first-frame latency after un-occlusion would come from libghostty's own opaque internal Metal loop, not from anything Workroom's code adds or could measure without an actual spike/instrumented test.
- **Re-mounting an ALREADY-CREATED surface is cheap**: `viewDidMoveToWindow()`'s `if surface == nil { createSurface() }` gate (~line 472) means re-homing a background tab's surface into a new container does NOT re-spawn the PTY/shell (`createSurface`, lines 235-313, is skipped entirely) — it only rewires occlusion/key-window observers, calls `updateWindowVisibility()`, and `updateMetalLayerSize()` (re-pushes content-scale/display-id/size for the new window). Claims first responder only if `wantsFocus == true` — for a hover preview, mount with `wantsFocus == false` so it structurally cannot steal focus.
- `TerminalContainerView.mount(in:)` (lines 72-95) is the exact re-homing shape to copy for a new minimal preview host: frame + `.autoresizingMask` (NOT AutoLayout constraints — the existing comment explains AutoLayout constraints to a stale container previously caused a real bug, issue #3, blank pane on split↔solo transitions). Do NOT reuse `TerminalContainerView` itself directly, since its `applyFocus` (lines 111-127) does first-responder bookkeeping irrelevant/risky for a hover-only mount — write a small dedicated host that only does the mount half.
- No `CAMetalLayer` exists in Workroom's own Swift (confirmed via full-repo grep) — libghostty's closed-source embedded macOS backend installs the real `CAMetalLayer` internally against the raw `NSView*` pointer handed over at `ghostty_surface_config_new()` (via `ghostty_platform_macos_s(nsview:)`). Once mounted+un-occluded in a real on-screen window, the surface's backing layer is genuinely part of that window's normal compositing tree — confirms an `SCContentFilter`/`SCStream` against that window sees it exactly as a human would; no offscreen/headless render path exists or is needed.

**Determining what's already on-screen** (`Core/TerminalSessions.swift`):
- `visibleTabIDs(for target:) -> [TerminalTab.ID]` (lines 588-594) + `isSplitVisible(for:)` (581-586) is the exact primitive: if a hovered tab's id is already in this set (e.g. it's a visible split member), it's ALREADY mounted and rendering — skip the whole re-home/un-occlude dance, just point capture at its existing on-screen region.
- `reconcileOcclusion(for target:)` (lines 1332-1339) is the CENTRAL occlusion-sync pass — sets `surface.setVisible(visible.contains(tab.id))` for every tab of a target, called from every state transition that changes what's on-screen (focus change, split, close, move, reap — 8+ call sites). **Real open design question**: if a hover-preview temporarily un-occludes a background tab's surface, and some UNRELATED state change fires `reconcileOcclusion` while the hover is active, it will call `setVisible(false)` on that surface since it's not in `visibleTabIDs` — the hover-preview's own un-occlusion would get silently clobbered mid-hover. Decide and state explicitly how v1 handles this (options: re-assert visibility after every reconcile pass via a hook/notification; give the hover-preview's un-occlusion its own tracked state that `reconcileOcclusion` is aware of and respects; or accept-and-document it as a known, low-stakes race for v1 since a hover is short-lived and a dropped frame or two is harmless — pick one and justify it, don't leave it unresolved).

**Cancellation pattern to use**: since the hover-preview's pipeline (mount → un-occlude → wait-for-first-frame → start SCStream → display frames → stop stream → re-occlude → detach) is a multi-step async sequence with real side effects on shared state (the surface, its window membership, its occlusion flag), and this codebase has an EMPIRICALLY MEASURED finding that SwiftUI's `.task(id:)` cancellation is NOT reliably delivered when a value swaps at a reused view-identity slot (`Views/Avatar.swift:232-294`'s own comment/workaround) — use the plain generation-counter pattern instead (`Core/WorkroomFileWatcher.swift:41,96,124-126` and `Core/GitHubAuthCache.swift:57,77-95` — bump an int generation when a new hover target is chosen, capture it before each async step, guard every continuation on `gen == self.generation` before touching the surface/stream). This should live on a plain class/controller, not as a SwiftUI `.task(id:)` closure, given the measured unreliability.

**Rendering the captured frames**: `AVSampleBufferDisplayLayer.enqueue(_:)` is the idiomatic way to display a continuous `CMSampleBuffer` feed with no manual per-frame `CGImage`/`NSImage` conversion — this would be the FIRST use of this API in this codebase, flag it as worth a small isolated spike/test rather than assuming it composes cleanly with the rest of the AppKit/SwiftUI view stack on the first try.

**Deliberately out of scope for v1** (already decided, don't re-litigate): full crop-math for capturing multiple regions from one shared window-wide stream (T12's `SnapshotSupport.swift` crop-math module still exists in git history at commit `8a1d2547`, reverted at `455d28e8`, if ever needed later) — for v1, size the `SCStream`'s captured region to just the small preview host's own bounds, one stream per active hover, no cropping needed at all.

## What I need from you
A concrete, staged implementation plan covering:
1. **New types/files needed** (e.g. a `TerminalHoverPreviewController` or similar owning the state machine + generation counter; a minimal preview-host NSView/NSViewRepresentable distinct from `TerminalContainerView`; wherever the SCStream/AVSampleBufferDisplayLayer plumbing lives) — propose concrete names and locations consistent with this codebase's existing organization (`Core/` for logic, `Views/` for SwiftUI).
2. **The exact state machine** for one hover session: idle → dwell-timer → (check `visibleTabIDs`, branch already-visible vs. needs-remount) → mount+unocclude (if needed) → start SCStream → first-frame-received → show preview UI → (hover ends) → stop stream → detach/re-occlude (if remounted) → idle. Be explicit about where the generation-counter guards go.
3. **Where hover/anchor state lives** and how the preview UI is positioned and hosted (recommend: SwiftUI overlay near the tab strip vs. a dedicated small NSPanel, with a concrete recommendation and why, given the `TerminalSearchBar` vs `SwitcherPanel` precedents above).
4. **Your resolution of the `reconcileOcclusion` race** described above — pick an approach and justify it.
5. **A stated v1 cut**: what's explicitly deferred (e.g. multi-hover queueing, crop-math sharing one stream across many chips, non-terminal tab types, measuring/optimizing cold-mount-to-first-frame latency beyond "log it and see") vs. what v1 must do.
6. **Verification plan**: how to confirm this actually works end-to-end (manual QA steps against a real running `Workroom Dev` build, what to look for, what would indicate the `reconcileOcclusion` race or first-frame latency is actually a problem in practice).

Do not write code. Produce a clear, sectioned implementation plan a senior engineer could execute from, citing the specific files/line-ranges above where you're building on them.

## 0. Critical finding — read this before the six sections

### 0.1 The bug: "copy `TerminalContainerView.mount(in:)`" reflows the pane

`TerminalContainerView.mount` (`macapp/WorkroomApp/Views/TerminalContainerView.swift:72-95`) does this on re-home:

```
view.frame = container.bounds                       // line 91
view.autoresizingMask = [.width, .height]            // line 92
```

`view` is the `GhosttySurfaceView`. Setting its frame fires `viewDidMoveToWindow` (`Core/GhosttySurfaceView.swift:456-500`), which unconditionally calls `updateMetalLayerSize()` (line 491). That function (lines 441-454) does:

```swift
if let backingSize = backingPixelSize() {                 // convertToBacking(bounds) — line 433-439
  ghostty_surface_set_size(surface, backingSize.width, backingSize.height)
}
```

`bounds` here is the **surface view's own frame** — whatever `container.bounds` was just set to. If the preview host container is sized to the small thumbnail footprint (e.g. 200×120), this pushes a small `ghostty_surface_set_size`, libghostty recomputes cols/rows, and the running program gets a real resize (`SIGWINCH`/reflow) — the exact outcome `QA-libghostty.md:18-19` documents as the app's normal, working resize behavior, and exactly what this feature must never trigger.

**The fix is a rule, not a redesign:** whatever code re-parents the surface for a preview must never write `view.frame`, `view.bounds`, or `autoresizingMask` on the `GhosttySurfaceView`. The surface keeps whatever size it already has (its last on-screen pane size, or the 800×480 default from `ensureSurfaceCreated`, `GhosttySurfaceView.swift:322-334`, for a tab that was never mounted). The thumbnail's *small* footprint has to come from something downstream of the surface, never from the surface's own geometry.

### 0.2 The deeper problem this forces onto the SCStream plan: where does the real-size surface actually sit?

Given 0.1, an `SCStream` capture of "the small preview box" doesn't work directly — the surface inside it must stay at its real (often much larger) size to avoid a resize call, which means the *capturable region* has to be the surface's full real bounds, and `SCStreamConfiguration.width/height` (small) does the shrinking at the frame-delivery level, exactly as the brief's own note says ("scales output independently of the source's real point size").

That in turn means the thing SCStream captures — a window (`SCContentFilter(desktopIndependentWindow:)`) — must itself be real-size, on an actual screen, and **not occluded by opaque siblings**, or `NSWindow.occlusionState` drops `.visible` → `GhosttySurfaceView.updateWindowVisibility()` (lines 531-536) → `applyOcclusionState()` → `ghostty_surface_set_occlusion(surface, false)` → nothing renders, nothing to capture. `SwitcherPanel.swift:53-57`'s own comment is exactly this mechanism from the other side ("`NSWindow.occlusionState` counts only OPAQUE coverage").

So the SCStream path needs a **dedicated, real-size, genuinely on-screen, unoccluded floating window per active hover** to host the surface in, separate from the small visible thumbnail badge under the chip. That's workable (place it off in a corner of the same screen, `.floating` level, ordered frontmost so nothing covers it) but it is real, fragile plumbing: multi-display placement, Stage Manager/Spaces, a notification banner transiently covering the corner, screen-locked/no-display edge cases — any of which can flip `occlusionState` and silently freeze the preview mid-hover, for reasons that have nothing to do with this feature's own code.

### 0.3 A materially simpler alternative worth a half-day spike first

A small host `NSView` with:
- `layer?.masksToBounds = true`
- `layer?.sublayerTransform = CATransform3DMakeScale(scale, scale, 1)` where `scale = thumbnailSize / surface.frame.size` (computed from the surface's *current, untouched* frame — never resized)
- the real `GhosttySurfaceView` added as its subview **without touching `.frame`/`.autoresizingMask`**

composites the surface's live `CAMetalLayer` output, scaled down, directly on screen — real pixels, zero re-encode, zero added latency, and critically: **it needs no separate real-size on-screen window**. The host itself can be small and live right where the thumbnail should appear (under the chip, in the *same* window as everything else), because the scaling is a compositing transform on an ancestor layer, not a capture of separately-hosted real estate. This deletes: the `ScreenCaptureKit` dependency, the `project.yml` framework link, the whole video pipeline (`AVSampleBufferDisplayLayer`, first-frame-wait state), and — most importantly — the entire "where does the unoccluded real-size window live" problem in §0.2.

Unknowns that make this a spike, not a given: whether `sublayerTransform` on an ancestor correctly composites a `CAMetalLayer` installed by libghostty's closed-source backend (anchor-point/coordinate-origin math is the fiddly part — `GhosttySurfaceView` has no `isFlipped` override, confirmed by grep, so it's standard bottom-left-origin AppKit, which affects the transform+position math); and whether libghostty keeps its render loop running when the view's on-screen visible area is small (it should, since occlusion is our own explicit `ghostty_surface_set_occlusion` call, not visibility-derived, but worth confirming empirically rather than assumed).

### 0.4 Recommendation

Spike §0.3 first (a throwaway branch, a few hours: one hovered chip, one hardcoded transform, confirm it renders live and scaled with no resize event). If it works, it should be the v1 architecture — it satisfies "pixel-identical, genuinely live, geometry never touched" more directly than a capture-and-redisplay pipeline, and removes real operational risk. If it fails (Metal backend doesn't tolerate the transform, or the composited output is visually wrong), fall back to the SCStream plan below with the "dedicated parking window" made explicit as its own tracked risk.

The six sections below build out the plan **as asked, for the SCStream/`AVSampleBufferDisplayLayer` architecture**, corrected for §0.1, with the §0.2 parking-window problem named as an explicit open risk rather than glossed over — and each stage notes where §0.3 would simplify or delete it outright, so whichever fork is chosen the plan doesn't need to be re-derived from scratch.
